newsitem.title: USA: IBP Inc to cut back Iowa hog operations.
newsitem.headline: IBP Inc to cut back Iowa hog operations.

text.p: IBP Inc said Monday it would significantly scale back operations at two of its Iowa pork plants starting next month.
IBP will cease second shift operations at its Columbus Junction, Iowa, hog plant effective March 3. It will end slaughter and most processing at its Council Bluffs, Iowa plant on April 24.

"This is an extremely difficult decision, given our investment in these plants and the hundreds of employees who depend upon these operations for their livelihood," Richard Bond, president of IBP's fresh meats division, said in a statement.
About 400 of the Columbus Junction plant's 1,500 employees and about 650 of the 1,200 Council Bluffs employees will be affected by the cutbacks, IBP said.
Declining hog supplies and industry overcapacity prompted IBP to scale back operations, IBP said.

"Due to the migration of hog supplies to southern states, there simply are no longer enough hogs available in today's marketplace to consistently meet the current production needs of the Midwestern pork processing industry," Bond said.
Market sources estimated daily capacity of the Columbus Junction plant at 13,000 head and the Council Bluffs plant at 7,500.
IBP said six million fewer hogs were expected to be available for marketing this year in Iowa and neighboring states than three years ago.
Hog marketings in the region are projected to total 49.4 million hogs in 1997, an 11 percent decline from the 55.6 million marketed in 1994, the release said.
"The number of hogs relative to available production capacity still remains out of balance," Bond said.
IBP officials also said further cutbacks were possible if the supply situation gets tighter.
"If hog numbers continue to decline, we will obviously have to look at scaling back operations elsewhere," Gary Mickelson, an IBP spokesman, said.

Larry Shipley, IBP executive vice president of corporate development, said in the statement, "Without sufficient local supplies of quality livestock, there isn't much reason to operate a packing plant."
IBP officials said they would not rule out resuming full operations at both plants eventually.
"If hog numbers rebound in the Midwest, these operations will be back up and running. If not, we will move on," Bond said.
IBP also operates hog plants in Perry, Storm Lake and Waterloo, Iowa, along with hog facilities at Logansport, Indiana, and Madison, Nebraska.
